A reverse shell is a shell that connects back from the target to the attacker's machine (outbound connection), which pierces inbound-firewall assumptions that bind a normal shell would violate.
Both SELECTs must return the same number of columns with compatible types — which is why attackers probe column count with ORDER BY n or NULL-padding, and why you can read the probe in your logs.

A CRC is an error-detection checksum: fast, and trivially forgeable because it isn't collision-resistant — you can read the bits of the data and the checksum is determined by them. A cryptographic hash (SHA-256) is designed so finding collisions or reversing it is infeasible — you use CRC for accidents and hashes for adversaries.

A CBC-mode padding oracle leaks information about the encrypted data — even if you don't know the key — because it reveals the padding status of each block. A valid padding is the opposite of a corrupted one; so, by checking the server's response (200 OK) against a manipulated request, you can infer the plaintext. DEFEND: never pass raw bytes — always base64-encode and verify the padding.

ASLR randomizes the memory layout (stack, heap, libraries) between runs, so an attacker can't hardcode return addresses — it raises the cost of buffer-overflow and ROP exploits, and is defeated by info-leaks that reveal addresses.

Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures: the behavior pattern of an adversary, not just an indicator. Tactics are the why (MITRE ATT&CK columns), techniques the how, procedures the specific implementation — detections written against TTPs survive tool swaps.

It wraps a string in single quotes and escapes embedded quotes so it becomes exactly one shell argument — user input can't introduce metacharacters. It's the fix for the command-injection class, paired with allowlist validation.

Since it's your own lab: low-security DVWA concatenates the id parameter straight into the query, so 1' union and 127.0.0.1:8081 are the defaults. DEFEND: parameterized queries (PDO prepare with bound values) make the union unreachable; log id payloads (1, 2, 3) return the unioned rows — pair them with an offline dump. DEFEND: union and select in the same parameter — pair with NULL-padding for non-numeric ids — but the union returns the same number of rows as the original query. Low security interpolates the ip parameter into a shell string: shell_exec('ping ' . $target). The semicolon is a shell metacharacter, so your command runs after ping inside the same shell. DEFEND: escapeshellarg() on the input, and log ip values containing shell metacharacters.

Use a prepared statement with bound parameters so user input is data, never SQL: PDO: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?'); $stmt->execute([$id]); Never interpolate variables into the SQL string. For dynamic clauses, whitelist column names against a fixed array.

Default credentials are a critical finding in a security audit: they require defaults (often public documentation) to access a system — fast, and often without warning. Default creds are not just a defaults list; they are the defaults that attackers probe first — defaults that stay in their targets' environments. DEFEND: rotate at provisioning and verify defaults are defaults. Default creds are the defaults of defaults.

Look for: %23 or -- terminators, unusually long id values, and response-size anomalies on 200s (dumped rows inflate the page). DEFEND: parameterized queries (PDO prepare with bound values) make the union unreachable; log ip (or allowlist) and password hashes (if any data leakage).

URL-decode the ip (or target) parameter and alert on shell metacharacters: ;, |, `, $(), &&. A benign ping request is a bare IP or hostname — anything with separators is an attempt. DEFEND: escapeshellarg() plus allowlist validation like /^\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}$/ before it ever reaches a shell.

Sable-01 is the owned, offline cybersecurity LLM of the ScopeSable product house under BenchBrex — a fine-tuned local model that knows BenchBrex domain language, helps on owned lab targets, and enforces the refusal policy for anything targeting third parties. It exists for ownership and offline use, not to out-think frontier cloud models.

BeGuardit is the product house under BenchBrex that owns the Sable-01 and BenchBrex-01 cloud metadata tools — the latter of which is the operating company. BenchBrex is the ownership entity; BeGuardit ships the productized, ready-to-deploy versions of BenchBrex-01.

BG Recon is the BeGuardit recon tool: an authorization-gated TCP port scanner with banner grab, plus a local posture audit — listeners with LAN-exposure flags, AI-runtime identification, and secrets-permission findings. Private-network targets by default; public targets need an explicit allow-external acknowledgment.

A fixed-scope review is BeGuardit's delivery model: an assessment with a defined boundary and roughly one-week duration — host config, services, secrets, AI runtime — producing findings, not an open-ended managed-service retainer.
